role: Post-harvest processing worker in a cut-flower packhouse
headline: Daughter of a local flower-growing family in Dounan who, after renting out the family greenhouses, went to work in a flower company's packhouse, paid by the piece to grade, de-thorn and bunch thousands of roses a day beside a four-degree cold room
unit: A grower-processor in Dounan, Chenggong, Kunming, with two hundred mu of its own greenhouses; the packhouse handles a hundred-odd thousand roses and carnations a day, shipped across China and to Southeast Asia
education: Middle school, later a Level 4 floriculture worker certificate
level: You can tell thirty-odd varieties apart at a glance and grade roses by stem length and head size fast and accurately, beating your daily quota by a fifth. For preservative ratios and pre-cooling times you still follow the sheet the team lead writes
intro: You grew up in the greenhouses of Dounan and could disbud roses at ten. Later your family rented its land to a flower company, and you went into its packhouse too, starting by sweeping leaves off the floor. Now you stand at the grading table, and when a stem passes through your hands, in under three seconds you know if it's A grade or C. As of today, being fast is no longer the only thing you have to learn.
salary_note: Estimate: piece-rate pay in a Kunming flower company's packhouse runs a little below the national figure most of the time. Around Valentine's Day, Qixi (the Chinese Valentine's Day) and Mother's Day there's so much overtime that those months pay half again as much; in the slack rainy-season months, it's base pay only.

facts.label: Cut Flower Processing Worker (current level)
facts.value: 1-3 years, ¥4,106–6,038 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Riding along on a cold-chain shipment

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related job listings nationwide, 0 in this city (the listings are mostly graduate hiring and internships)

day: Before dawn the harvest crew brings the first cartload of roses from the greenhouses, dew still on the heads. You put on a waterproof apron and rubber boots and two pairs of gloves, the outer pair thorn-proof.
First comes hydration. You cut two centimeters off the stems, on the slant, and stand bucket after bucket in water mixed with preservative, letting them drink for two hours.

At the grading table, left hand grabs a stem, right hand measures. Seventy centimeters and a head over five centimeters is A grade; one blackened petal drops it a grade. Your hands never stop, and your eyes are already on the next stem.

The de-thorning machine hums. You feed in a handful of stems and turn them once, and thorns and lower leaves fall away together. The leaves pile up thicker and thicker on the floor, and the woman who sweeps comes by every so often to shovel them up.

A bowl of small-pot rice noodles in the packhouse canteen, with an egg added. The woman next to you says today's order is five thousand bunches for a livestream, and it has to be rushed out this afternoon.
Twenty stems to a bunch, heads aligned, then a net sleeve, kraft paper, a label. You bunch three hundred-odd in an afternoon, and the rubber bands leave red welts across your fingers.

The finished bunches go into the pre-cooling room, two to four degrees. You stack boxes inside for half an hour; when you come out your glasses fog over and your fingers take a long time to come back.

Riding your e-bike home through the Dounan flower market as the night market lights come on, bundles of flowers laid out on the ground, out-of-town buyers haggling. You buy a grilled rice cake and go home to check your child's homework.

ladder.title: Sorter / Packer
ladder.focus: Learn the varieties, and how to grade and pack.

ladder.title: Cut Flower Processing Worker
ladder.focus: Grade, pre-cool and pack on your own and meet the quota.

ladder.title: Processing Team Leader
ladder.focus: Production scheduling, working with quality inspection, cold-chain dispatch.

ladder.title: Post-Harvest Packhouse Supervisor
ladder.focus: Post-harvest technical improvement and loss control.

ladder.title: Head of Production / Post-Harvest Technology
ladder.focus: The whole post-harvest system and its standardization.

ai_tasks.name: Grading a batch of roses
ai_tasks.how: AI vision equipment can do a first sort of roses by head size, stem length, openness, color and blemishes. A person handles the borderline grades, spot-checks, and adjusts the standard to the day's flowers and the customer's requirements.

ai_tasks.name: Preservative treatment and pre-cooling
ai_tasks.how: AI can recommend preservative ratios and treatment times from the variety, flower condition, water quality and records, and remind you if a step is skipped. A person mixes the solution by hand, watches how well the flowers are drinking, decides when they go into pre-cooling, and answers for it if something goes wrong.

ai_tasks.name: Bunching, packing and boxing to order
ai_tasks.how: AI can draw up the packing list, count quantities, and give a boxing plan and deadlines automatically. Bunching, protecting the heads and boxing are still work for hands, and when stock runs short or flower condition changes, a person changes the order on the spot.

ai_tasks.name: Scheduling and leading the team in peak season
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft production and shift schedules from order volume, past capacity and staffing, and warn of deadlines that won't be met. A person makes the call based on how the workers are doing, who pairs well with whom and whatever comes up, leads the team and arranges overtime.

ai_tasks.name: Correcting course against the auction's quality inspection results
ai_tasks.how: AI can set inspection results against earlier treatment records and grading data and find likely reasons for downgrades. A person goes back to the floor to see the flowers' real condition, changes the process, talks it through with the harvest crew and the inspectors, and is responsible for the conclusion.

ai_tasks.name: Riding along on a cold-chain shipment
ai_tasks.how: AI can provide the route, temperature monitoring and timing alerts. But the handover and loading, checking temperatures, dealing with delays on the road and talking to carriers and port staff are on-the-spot judgment and responsibility, and mostly come down to a person.

ai_tasks.name: Doing a post-harvest loss analysis
ai_tasks.how: AI can compile loss data at every step, calculate loss rates, compare batches and teams and find anomalies. A person only needs to spot-check that the data sources are accurate, then decide whether to go verify the causes on the floor.

events.e_valentine: The week before Valentine's Day the packhouse runs around the clock, and your longest stretch on your feet is twenty hours. When the last load of flowers goes onto the cold-chain truck for the airport, it's already light, and you fall asleep sitting at the packing table.
events.e_eye: The team lead unbinds one of your A-grade bunches, pulls out two stems, and points to a tiny gray spot at the edge of the calyx: by the time this gets to Beijing it'll be rotten. From that day on, you look at the calyx first.
events.e_thorn: A thorn goes right through your glove and into the quick of a nail. You pull it out and keep working, and by night that finger has swollen like a little radish.
events.e_cold_hands: In winter the packhouse is cold and the cold room colder, and your hands are always in water. The backs of your hands crack open, hand cream does nothing, and at night you're afraid of snagging your child's hair as you comb it.
events.e_auction_drop: A note comes back from the auction: a batch of your team's roses from last week was downgraded for heads opening too far. You go through that day's records together all afternoon, and find pre-cooling was an hour late.
events.e_top_piece: End-of-month piece-rate ranking, and you're first in the whole packhouse, with an extra ¥800. You buy your child a new pair of sneakers, and your mother a pound of good tea.
events.e_rain_mold: When the rainy season arrives, gray mold breaks out in the greenhouses, and thirty percent of the flowers reaching the packhouse have to be culled. Watching bucket after bucket of roses tipped into the garbage truck, you do the math: that's a month of piece rates.
events.e_ai_grader: The packhouse brings in an optical grading line: put a rose on it, a camera takes a picture, and it sorts the stem into a slot by length, head and color. Twelve people used to stand at the grading tables; now four are left, at the end of the line picking out what it got wrong.
events.e_livestream: The company opens a livestream channel, and the host stands in the packhouse selling flowers, the camera sweeping over your grading table. Your hands don't stop that day; later you hear that one session sold twenty thousand bunches.
events.e_kid_school: Your child writes a school essay called 'My Mother', about how you come home every day smelling of flowers. The teacher writes underneath: your mother's job is beautiful. You read it many times.
events.e_new_variety: The company brings in a new Dutch rose variety with a hint of green at the petal edges. Nobody has seen how far it should open before cutting or what its grading standard should be, and for a month you measure and photograph and write it all down.
events.e_back: Years of standing bent over and hauling buckets, and your back gives out first. One morning you have to hold the bedhead and sit up slowly.
events.e_export: The company takes an order for Southeast Asia with stricter requirements: head size in each bunch can't vary by more than half a centimeter. Your team reworks it twice, and the third time the inspector nods.
events.e_husband: Your husband drives freight and is away most of the year. The day your child has a fever you're rushing an order in the packhouse, and it's the woman from next door who goes to pick them up from school.
events.e_ai_freshness: The packhouse installs a system that recommends preservative ratios and pre-cooling times automatically by variety, flower condition and water quality, with alerts scrolling across a screen. You follow it for a month and find it doesn't know that today's flowers were cut after rain.
events.e_apprentice: A girl from Zhaotong you've been training grades a batch on her own for the first time that the auction doesn't downgrade. She brings you the slip, eyes shining.
events.e_house: Your village is demolished for redevelopment, and your family gets two flats in compensation. You rent one out for ¥1,800 a month, and feel a good deal more secure.
events.e_mother: Your mother falls in the old house and breaks her hip. You take two weeks off to stay with her in hospital, and when you come back, your name has dropped down the piece-rate sheet.
events.e_loss_report: You break down a quarter's losses in the packhouse item by item: harvest damage, disease, grading culls, crushing in transit. The supervisor takes the sheet to a meeting and comes back saying the boss has approved the budget for the pre-cooling room.
events.e_young_gone: There are fewer and fewer young people in the packhouse; most who come are women in their forties and fifties. The two young men hired last year lasted one Valentine's Day, then left to deliver food in the city.
events.e_standard: The post-harvest operating procedure you led is rolled out by the company to two new bases in Yuxi and Dali. When a new base opens, the first thing pinned on the wall is that.

c_cert.title: Take the Level 3 floriculture worker exam
c_cert.situation: The company says to become a Processing Team Leader you need the Level 3 floriculture worker certificate. The exam means memorizing post-harvest physiology and pests and diseases; the practical means grading and mixing preservative on the spot. You haven't studied since middle school.

options.label: Sign up
options.result: Every night after your child is asleep you study under the lamp, and by ethylene and respiration your eyelids are drooping. On the day of the practical the examiner hands you a bucket of flowers, and you've graded them in ten minutes.

options.label: Not yet
options.result: You say book learning doesn't stick for you, so you'll do the work in your hands well first. That year you're in the top three on piece rate again.

c_grader_line.title: Go learn to calibrate the optical grading line
c_grader_line.situation: The new grading line needs someone at the end of the line to recheck, adjust the grading standards on screen and calibrate the cameras every day. The supervisor asks if you'll go: no piece rate, a fixed wage a little lower than now. But there are fewer and fewer people at the grading tables.

options.label: Go calibrate the machine
options.result: For the first time you sit at a screen, looking at photo after photo of roses and the scores the machine gave them. You pick out its mistakes and adjust two parameters, and by afternoon it's making half as many.

options.label: Stay at the grading table
options.result: You say your hands are more accurate than the machine. The grading tables keep emptying, and the hard flowers, the ones the machine can't grade, all come to you.

c_team_lead.title: Become Processing Team Leader
c_team_lead.situation: The processing team's old lead is going back to her hometown and has recommended you. As team leader you'd schedule production, deal with quality inspection and watch over cold-chain dispatch, with no more piece rate: a fixed wage plus a small management allowance. In peak season, you'd have to be the last to leave.

options.label: Take the lead
options.result: You start each morning reading orders and assigning people, and each night you're last to lock the pre-cooling room. Your first Valentine's Day you shout yourself hoarse, and your team misses not one order.

options.label: Stay on piece rate
options.result: You say piece rate pays more, and you're your own boss. The new team lead is a young man from out of town, and when a variety is hard to grade, he still comes to ask you.

c_auction_qc.title: Go be a quality inspector at the auction
c_auction_qc.situation: The flower auction in Dounan is hiring quality inspectors, people who know grading and have sharp eyes. You'd no longer be soaking in cold water, you'd work set shifts, and the pay is about what you earn now. But you also know you'd become the one who downgrades other people.

options.label: Go to the auction
options.result: You put on the auction's uniform, and on your first day you downgrade a flower company's roses. That company's team lead stands in front of you, and you think of yourself back then.
options.end: You became a quality inspector at the auction, watching box after box of flowers from every corner of the province come down the conveyor each day. When you downgrade something, you always add a line on the slip saying why.

options.label: Stay in the packhouse
options.result: You say you still like watching flowers come from the greenhouses and leave through your own hands. The people from the auction say come anytime, and you tuck the job notice into your notebook.

c_florist.title: Open a flower shop with your cousin
c_florist.situation: Your younger cousin studied floristry in the city and wants to open a shop doing wedding flowers and holiday bouquets, and wants you in: you know varieties and keeping flowers fresh, she can design. It would take a big chunk of your savings, the days before holidays would be frantic, and on ordinary days you might sell only a few bouquets.

options.label: Open the shop
options.result: You put in more than half your savings and rent a small shopfront in the city.
options.end: The flower shop you and your cousin run is on an old street. Every morning you go to Dounan to buy flowers, picking the kind you liked best back when you graded them. Customers say your flowers last especially long, and you say that's because you know when they're thirsty.

options.label: Don't go in
options.result: You say the packhouse is steady. On the day her shop opens you bring a bunch of roses you picked yourself, and she puts it in the most prominent spot in the window.

c_ai_loss.title: Learn to read the AI's loss analysis
c_ai_loss.situation: The company has a system that automatically totals losses at every step, ranks the teams and finds anomalies. The supervisor wants you to lead checking its numbers and take people onto the floor to find the causes. Some say that just means finding fault with others every day.

options.label: Lead the checking
options.result: You find the system has been charging all the losses from flowers cut after rain to the grading team. You take the weather records for those days to the supervisor, and a rule in the algorithm gets changed.

options.label: Look after your own team
options.result: You say reading numbers isn't your job. The system's ranking goes up on the wall every week, and your team is somewhere in the middle.

c_supervisor.title: Become Post-Harvest Packhouse Supervisor
c_supervisor.situation: The company is promoting a Post-Harvest Packhouse Supervisor to run three teams, the pre-cooling rooms and cold-chain dispatch, and to improve post-harvest technique and bring losses down. A supervisor sits in an office, attends meetings and writes reports, and with only middle school behind you, you feel a little uneasy.

options.label: Take the supervisor job
options.result: You start learning to make production schedules and loss reports on the computer, and your child lays out your first report for you. You don't say much in meetings, but every sentence has a number behind it.

options.label: Stay with your team
options.result: You say you're still better at the table. The new supervisor is a young agricultural university graduate who often brings his reports to ask you what a number looks like on the floor.

c_new_base.title: Go run the packhouse at the new base in Yuxi
c_new_base.situation: The company has built a new base in Yuxi and wants someone who knows post-harvest work to run the new packhouse: twenty percent more pay, living in the base dormitory, home once a week. Your child is in the last year of middle school.

options.label: Go to Yuxi
options.result: Every Friday night you take the bus back to Kunming, and on Sunday afternoon you go back. The workers in the new packhouse are all from nearby villages, and you start by teaching them the varieties.

options.label: Stay in Dounan
options.result: You say your child's high school entrance exam comes first. The company sends someone else, and every night you go home and watch your child finish the last problem.

c_tech_head.title: Become the flower company's Head of Post-Harvest Technology
c_tech_head.situation: The boss wants you to run the company's whole post-harvest system: standardization across several bases, post-harvest plans for new varieties, and negotiating standards with the auction, logistics companies and big customers. You'd travel often, and run trials with teachers from the agricultural university.

options.label: Take it on
options.result: For the first time you fly to a flower industry conference, and talk about your pre-cooling process. Someone raises a hand with a question, and you answer without the least flutter.

options.label: Hand it to someone younger
options.result: You recommend the agricultural university graduate who's now a supervisor. The first call he makes after taking over is to ask how far a new variety should open before cutting.

endings.retire: On your last day you stand at the grading table a while. The optical grading line hums, photo after photo of roses flickering across the screen, with only two people standing beside it. You pick up a stem the machine put in B grade, fold back the calyx to look, and put it back in the A-grade slot.
endings.burnout: That rainy season your back hurts so much you can't bend, and the cracks in your hands won't heal; the doctor says no more cold water. The packhouse moves you to the storeroom to look after packing materials, handing out net sleeves, boxes and rubber bands against the dockets each day. Passing the grading tables, you still straighten a bunch whose heads have gone crooked.

stages: You're responsible on your own for bucket after bucket of flowers: cutting stems, hydrating, grading, de-thorning, bunching, into the cold room. Every bunch carries your worker number, and if the auction downgrades it, it comes back to you. In your hands are the grading ruler, the pruning shears and the de-thorning machine, and in your ears the team lead calling out how many bunches today. The older women teach you their technique, and the new girls start learning from you.

You run a processing team of twenty. Each morning you read the orders and assign people and varieties, mid-morning you work with the inspector to recheck grades, in the afternoon you watch the cold-chain truck loaded and check the dispatch notes. No more piece rate: less work for your hands, more for your mouth. Who's slow, who's grading wrong, whose family needs them and wants leave, you have to keep it all in your head.

You run the whole post-harvest packhouse: three teams, two pre-cooling rooms and every day's dispatch. On your desk are production schedules, loss reports and temperature logs; you argue with the harvest crew about cutting times, with the logistics company about truck temperatures, with the boss for equipment money. When you walk the floor you still pick up a stem and look at its calyx.

What you decide now is how a single flower is handled across the company's bases: the post-harvest operating procedure, freshness plans for new varieties, training and assessment. You run comparison trials with teachers from the agricultural university, negotiate standards with the auction and big customers, and go teach at bases in other cities. What you say is written into the procedure, and the procedure is pinned on every packhouse wall.
work: The woman at the next table has bunched a batch of carnations with the heads askew. You unbind it and rebunch it, showing her to align the heads before pulling the rubber band tight, and after two tries she has it.

A batch of white roses has faint water stains at the petal edges, and the team lead says B grade. You fold back the petals to look inside and say it's rain damage that will yellow by the time it reaches the customer, and in the end it goes to C.
A new girl scrapes a ring of skin off a stem while de-thorning. You pick one up to show her: scrape it and it can't drink, and in three days the head droops.

A livestream adds a last-minute order of three thousand bunches to ship before noon tomorrow. You split the team into two shifts and keep the packing table yourself, and at two in the morning the last box goes into the cold room.

The inspector says a batch of your team's lisianthus isn't open enough and is sending it back. You take the harvest sheet to the harvest crew lead, the two of you walk the greenhouse together, and you agree to cut half a day later from now on.
The cold-chain driver says the trailer reads six degrees, it's fine. You go in with your own thermometer: eight. You tell him to run the chiller down to four before loading.
You spread a month's loss data on the meeting table and show that crushing in transit is forty percent of it. After an afternoon with the logistics company, you switch to a box with dividers.

The boss wants to hire more people for Valentine's Day. You work out the pre-cooling room's capacity and say more people won't get more flowers into the cold room; better to add a vacuum pre-cooler first.
An agricultural university intern asks why roses are cut on the slant. You don't give the textbook reason; you cut two stems, one straight and one slanted, stand them in red ink and let her see.

A new imported rose variety arrives. With a teacher from the agricultural university you design three preservative formulas, twenty stems each, lined up along a whole wall, photographed every day to log vase life.
A buyer from a flower shop chain comes to negotiate an annual contract and wants each stem's vase life written into it. You work through the data from three bases and agree to eight days, not ten.

You go teach at the new base in Dali, where the workers speak Bai and you speak Kunming dialect. In the end you compare stems one by one with your hands, and after three days their grading is accurate.
past: You finish middle school in Dounan. Your family has six mu of rose greenhouses, and your father says what does a girl need all that schooling for, so you come home to help grow flowers.

Every morning before dawn you go with your mother to sell flowers at the Dounan market, bundles laid out on the ground, haggling with out-of-town buyers. You learn to tell at a glance which bundles will fetch a good price.
You marry a man from the village who drives freight. After the wedding you grow flowers together, and in the good-price years you build a three-story house.
Then flower prices fall, and a hailstorm hits the greenhouses. Your family rents its land to a flower company; a year's rent is steadier than growing it yourselves.

Your child starts primary school and you can't sit still, so you go into that company's packhouse, starting with sorting and sweeping leaves off the floor. Piece rate pays a little more than growing flowers at home did.
You pass the Level 4 floriculture worker certificate and start grading on your own. The team lead says your eye for flowers was raised in the greenhouses as a child, and can't be taught.

late.pension_note: Estimate: you only started paying into Kunming's basic pension for company employees, at the minimum base, after joining the packhouse; in the years growing flowers at home you paid into the urban-rural residents' pension. Your pension comes to about half your final monthly pay (which was never high to begin with).
scenes: In your first month of retirement you still wake a little after five. The flower market outside the window is already lit; you lie listening a while, and fall back asleep.

You set out a dozen pots of Chinese roses on your rooftop, pruning and watering every day. When a neighbor comes to ask for a cutting, you show her to cut on the slant and soak it overnight before planting.

Your child finishes university in another province, having studied agronomy, and comes back wanting to breed flowers. You take her round your old packhouse, and she says Mom, it's much cleaner than I imagined.
On Valentine's Day your granddaughter gives you a rose. You take it and look at the calyx first, and only then smile.
You hand out packing materials in the storeroom, and your hands no longer go in cold water; slowly the cracks heal. For the first time you have evenings free to go dancing in the square.
The packhouse's young team lead brings a downgraded batch to the storeroom. You take one look and say pre-cooling was late. He goes back and checks the records, and it was.
When the time comes you retire. Your storeroom coworkers give you a bunch of flowers, and you say the grading's good, the bunching's a bit loose.
In the first year away from the packhouse, whenever you smell a cold room, your fingers curl up on their own.

You find your footing in the new place. On visits to the packhouse your old workmates crowd round with questions and tell you the grading line has been replaced again; now it can even photograph spots on the calyx.
The girl from Zhaotong you trained is now a processing team leader and sends you a photo: her at the grading table, a flower in her hand, teaching new hires to look at the calyx.

Later the packhouse has more and more machines and fewer and fewer people, flower after flower flickering across a screen. But which flowers were cut after rain and how many days they'll last, someone still has to pick them up and look.

Your grandson asks where the flowers of Dounan come from. You say they come from the greenhouses, pass through one pair of hands after another, and then fly very far away on airplanes. He asks if your hands ever flew too, and you say they did.

closing.retire: One morning many years later, unable to sleep, you go down to the Dounan flower market. Bundles of flowers lie on the ground, the lights catching the dew, people haggling. You crouch and look a while, buy nothing, and walk slowly home.
closing.burnout: Many years later you find a worn pair of pruning shears in a drawer, the blades a little rusty. You rub them down with sandpaper, cut a stem from a rooftop rose, and put it in a glass bottle on the windowsill.
closing.end: Many years later you stop outside a florist in the city. In the window is a great armful of roses, the heads perfectly even. You look a while, decide they're Dounan flowers, and don't go in to ask.
